name: United States
summary_text:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The order also mandated that federal agencies use "sex" rather than "gender," required removal of materials that promote what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces.
 The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The X marker had been available since 2022. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992; the Human Rights Campaign records that the policy remains challenged in federal courts. The ACLU sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.
 Entry screening carries its own exposure. On 5 February 2025 an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. Separately, the Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.
 Facilities rules vary sharply by state. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, and some states make trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law; civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.
 Identity documents at state level are also being closed. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures, with further targeting bills pending. Equality-map research shows the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state.
 Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.
 Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.
 Care access is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation, and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and in October 2025 proposed health-department rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
 Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

sources.title: Executive Order of January 20, 2025 - Trump gender recognition order
sources.documents: Directs U.S. government to remove federal protections for transgender individuals and remove recognition of transgender identity; declares only male and female genders recognized, official documents must reflect biological sex assigned at birth; bans trans military service and halts financing for gender-affirming care under 19.
sources.detail: No URL visible in text; cited as issued January 20, 2025, beginning of Donald Trump's second presidency

Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

summary_text:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The order also mandated that federal agencies use "sex" rather than "gender," required removal of materials that promote what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces.
 The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The X marker had been available since 2022. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992; the Human Rights Campaign records that the policy remains challenged in federal courts. The ACLU sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.
 Entry screening carries its own exposure. On 5 February 2025 an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. Separately, the Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.
 Facilities rules vary sharply by state. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, and some states make trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law; civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.
 Identity documents at state level are also being closed. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures, with further targeting bills pending. Equality-map research shows the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state.
 Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.
